n: Jailhouse Rock, by Elvis Presley, 1957, from his movie of the same name.
Rock and roll, written by Leiber and Stoller.
Listen for the hard, stop time hits that open each verse.
items.lyr: The warden throws a party in the county jail, and the prisoners' band plays so well that everybody dances. It's a comic scene full of nicknames for the inmates, with the whole cell block dancing.

n: Blue Suede Shoes, by Elvis Presley, 1956, his cover of the Carl Perkins song.
Listen for how much more he leans into the vocal, and the hip shaking stage energy.
items.lyr: The same lyrics as Carl Perkins's version: do anything to me, but don't step on my blue suede shoes.

n: Tutti Frutti, by Little Richard, 1955.
Listen for the pounding piano and his shrieks.
items.lyr: "Tutti frutti" is an ice cream flavor, and "a-wop-bop-a-loo-bop" is pure rhythm with no meaning. He sings about two girls, Sue and Daisy, who drive him wild. The original lyrics were much ruder and were cleaned up before recording.

n: Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On, by Jerry Lee Lewis, 1957.
Rockabilly piano, from the man nicknamed The Killer.
Listen for the sweeping glissandos in his right hand, the pounding left hand, and his wild stage antics.
items.lyr: An invitation to a party where "there's a whole lotta shakin' goin' on": everyone's dancing, and it's also a sexual double meaning. He tells his partner to come along and shake, with spoken asides that egg the crowd on.

n: Chapter one: Roots of Rock Music.

The point of this chapter is where rock's ingredients came from: older American popular music, and above all the blues, which combined West African and European traditions, and which recording technology and radio finally spread to everyone.

America's first popular songs came from British and other European settlers, and the popular music industry grew through the eighteen hundreds and exploded in the twentieth century with the phonograph, radio, and television.
Four styles, all established by the 1890s, directly influenced rock: ragtime, Tin Pan Alley, the blues, and jazz.
Ragtime and Tin Pan Alley were composed and sold as sheet music, while the blues and jazz were improvised, and because the first jazz and blues recordings came late, their earliest forms are lost.
Ragtime was mainly, though not only, an African American style.
It was named for the ragged, or syncopated, melody played by the pianist's right hand, while the left hand steadily alternated between a single bass note and a chord.
Its best known composer was Scott Joplin (Scott. Joplin.), 1868 to 1917, whose Maple Leaf Rag sold more than a million copies of sheet music.
Ragtime influenced rock through its energy and syncopated rhythms, and through stride piano, which developed from it and became part of many rhythm and blues piano styles.
Maple Leaf Rag, by Scott Joplin (Scott. Joplin.). Ragtime, 1899.

items.s: Take Me Out to the Ball Game
n: Tin Pan Alley was the street in New York where many music publishers had their offices in the late eighteen hundreds and early nineteen hundreds, named for the tinny sound of their cheap upright pianos.
Their songs were sentimental ballads or fun, escapist songs, often based on popular dance rhythms, and above all simple and easy to remember, like Take Me Out to the Ball Game, from 1908.

These catchy melodies became the model for pop oriented rock songs, ballads, and dance music, with one difference: Tin Pan Alley was sold as sheet music for people to play themselves, while rock was sold as records.
Take Me Out to the Ball Game, by Billy Murray. Tin Pan Alley, 1908.

By the late eighteen hundreds, New Orleans bands played parades, funerals, picnics, and dances, and African American and Creole musicians began improvising on the written lines, adding African rhythms and influences from the blues and gospel.
This was called hot music, played by a front line of trumpet, clarinet, and trombone over a rhythm section, the instruments that keep the beat and play the chords.
Jazz stayed dance music through the swing era, from about 1934 to the end of World War Two, played by big bands from written arrangements.

Swing changed how the bass was played: instead of pumping between the first and third beats, swing bassists played a walking bass, a new note on every beat, later used in rhythm and blues and rock and roll.

Swing bands often backed singers in a new style called crooning, made possible by the microphone, which could amplify a soft, gentle voice: crooners slid from note to note for a warm, sentimental effect.
Bing Crosby (Bing. Crosby.) was one of the most popular crooners of the swing era.
Pennies from Heaven, by Bing Crosby (Bing. Crosby.). Crooner, 1936.
Perry Como was another crooner of the swing era, and crooners like him later influenced the teen idols of the late fifties and early sixties.
Prisoner of Love, by Perry Como. Crooner, 1946.
The earliest roots of the blues lie in Africa, but also in music from Arabia, the Middle East, and Moorish Spain.

The book finds the clearest African predecessor in the griots of Sierra Leone, oral poets who sang the history of their people, though the blues was different: the personal expression of people denied respect.
European church hymns gave the blues a three chord progression and short verses of equal length.

Slavery added work songs, sung by groups in the African call and response style, where a leader sings a phrase and the group answers, and field hollers, sung by one worker alone, slow, free in rhythm, and improvised.
Both sometimes used signifying, lyrics with a double meaning, a tradition that reappears in rap.
The earliest blues came from the rural South and is called country blues, sung by performers who accompanied themselves on guitar.
Most blues follows a form called the twelve bar blues.
The lyrics use an A A B pattern: the first line is sung, then repeated, and a contrasting third line answers it.
Each line lasts four bars of four beats, so a full verse, also called a chorus, is twelve bars.
Call and response is built into the form, because the singer stops early in each line and an instrument fills the rest as a response.
The chords follow a standard pattern of tonic, subdominant, and dominant chords.
The beat is usually divided unevenly, long short, long short, called a shuffle at slow tempos, while folk and country music divide the beat evenly.
The country blues style that most influenced rock was delta blues, from the Mississippi delta, rough and emotional.

Many delta guitarists slid a bottleneck along the strings, and the blues uses blue notes, the third and seventh notes of the scale lowered or bent in pitch, which a bottleneck or string bending can reach between the frets.
Delta musicians named in the book include Robert Johnson, Son House, and Charley Patton (Charley. Patton.).
We'll come back to Johnson. First, Charley Patton.
Pony Blues, by Charley Patton (Charley. Patton.). Delta blues, 1929.
Not every slide player used a bottleneck: Lead Belly (Lead. Belly.), Huddie Ledbetter, got a similar effect by sliding a knife along the strings.
Midnight Special, by Lead Belly (Lead. Belly.). Country blues, 1934.
Later musicians kept delta bottleneck guitar while updating it with amplification and other instruments, among them Big Joe Williams and Muddy Waters, whom we'll hear much more of in chapter two.
Muddy Waters began recording for Aristocrat Records, renamed Chess Records in 1948.
I Can't Be Satisfied, by Muddy Waters. Delta blues, 1948.
Cross Road Blues, by Robert Johnson, 1937.
Delta blues.
Johnson was a Mississippi singer and guitarist who recorded only twenty nine songs, and legend says he sold his soul at a crossroads to play so well.
Listen for his bottleneck slide guitar answering his voice, and his free rhythm, where he adds beats and sings in a different rhythm from the one he plays.
items.lyr: A Black man stands at a crossroads as the sun goes down, trying to wave down a passing car ("flag a ride"), but nobody stops for him. Sundown matters: in the 1930s South, African Americans could be in danger if they were caught outside after dark, so he is desperate to get away before night. He falls to his knees and asks God for mercy. Beyond the literal story, the song is about loneliness and having no way out.
nl: Robert Johnson (Robert. Johnson.), 1911 to 1938, was one of the most influential country blues singer guitarists of the thirties.
He grew up poor on a Mississippi plantation, and recorded only twenty nine songs, in makeshift studios in hotel rooms, barely distributed in his lifetime.
Later reissues made him a major influence on rock musicians, and stories from the few who heard him live gave rise to the myth that he sold his soul to play so well.

Johnson used the A A B lyrics and the basic blues chords, but he wasn't bound by strict rhythm: he added extra beats and bars, and sometimes sang in a different rhythm from the one he played on guitar.
Using more than one rhythm at the same time is called polyrhythm, a practice known in some African traditions.
The listening guide is Cross Road Blues, from 1937, four twelve bar choruses with no other musicians, in which Johnson answers his own singing on bottleneck guitar.
The tempo is about 88 beats per minute, but he speeds up and slows down at will.
The lyrics show a lonely black man in the 1930s South who can't flag a ride and must leave the crossroads before dark, a reference to the curfews imposed on African Americans at the time.
Two years after this recording, Johnson died at twenty seven, poisoned either by a woman he was involved with or by her husband.
Cross Road Blues, by Robert Johnson (Robert. Johnson.). Delta blues, 1937.

n: Many rock groups recorded Johnson's songs, including the Rolling Stones, Fleetwood Mac, and Cream, which recorded Cross Road Blues as Crossroads.
Crossroads, by Cream. Blues rock, 1968.
Most country blues singers who caught the record companies' attention were men, but women sang the blues too, in two different ways.
Some, like Memphis Minnie (Memphis. Minnie.), accompanied themselves on guitar in the country blues tradition.
When the Levee Breaks, by Memphis Minnie (Memphis. Minnie.). Country blues, 1929.
Others, called classic blues singers, didn't play an instrument, but sang in front of jazz bands, so they developed powerful, gutsy voices that could be heard over the band.
Most classic blues singers were from the South and grew up hearing country blues, and other classic blues singers included Alberta Hunter, Mamie Smith, and Ida Cox.
Two of them, Ma Rainey (Ma. Rainey.) and Bessie Smith, inspired later rock singers.
First, Ma Rainey.
See See Rider Blues, by Ma Rainey (Ma. Rainey.). Classic blues, 1924.
Lost Your Head Blues, by Bessie Smith, 1926.
Classic blues.
Smith was called the Empress of the Blues, a singer with a huge voice built to carry over a jazz band.
Listen for the cornet answering each of her lines, which is call and response, and the A A B pattern of the lyrics, where each first line is sung twice.
items.lyr: Her man has come into money, and now he's "lost his head," meaning he's become arrogant and foolish, and he's treating her badly. She tells him she was good to him when he was poor, and now she's leaving. "Once ain't for always, and two ain't for twice" is a proverb: don't expect to get away with the same thing twice. In the last verse her days feel lonely and her nights feel long.
nl: Bessie Smith (Bessie. Smith.), 1894 to 1937, earned the title Empress of the Blues.
She was featured in the 1929 film Saint Louis Blues, and she died from injuries in a car accident while on tour.
The listening guide is Lost Your Head Blues, from 1926, recorded with Joe Smith on cornet and Fletcher Henderson on piano.

It's a twelve bar blues with a four bar introduction and five choruses, in which the cornet plays the fill at the end of each vocal line, the call and response pattern again, while the piano accompanies without solos.
The lyrics are about money corrupting love: now that her man has money, he's deserting the woman who stood by him when he was poor.
Lost Your Head Blues, by Bessie Smith (Bessie. Smith.). Classic blues, 1926.

n: Ma Rainey and Bessie Smith inspired the rock singers Etta James, LaVern Baker, and Janis Joplin.
Here's Janis Joplin.
Piece of My Heart, by Janis Joplin. Blues rock, 1968.

Rock also grew from styles that weren't yet nationally popular: delta blues and rhythm and blues were mostly sold in African American neighborhoods, a division caused partly by racism and segregation.
Technology was essential.
Magnetic tape recorders improved sound quality and let studios create echo effects and overdubs, which means recording new parts on top of an existing recording.
Elvis Presley's Heartbreak Hotel, from 1956, is a famous example of echo.
Heartbreak Hotel, by Elvis Presley. Rock and roll, 1956.
Eddie Cochran's Summertime Blues, from 1958, is a famous example of overdubbing: he recorded his own playing several times, creating a sound he couldn't have made live without other musicians.
Summertime Blues, by Eddie Cochran. Rockabilly, 1958.

Three developments in 1948 were especially important: transistor radios, long playing albums, and forty five R P M singles, which let people buy a single song cheaply and filled the jukeboxes in soda fountains, restaurants, and bars.
Racial barriers began to erode when white teenagers started dancing to the rhythm and blues of jump bands like Louis Jordan and his Tympany Five in the late forties.
Choo Choo Ch'Boogie, by Louis Jordan. Jump blues, 1946.

In the late forties, small independent radio stations sprang up everywhere, with disc jockeys who weren't afraid to play rock and black rhythm and blues, and radio was how most white teenagers first heard it.
TV dance shows like American Bandstand later spread rock nationwide.

By 1951, the smooth sound of African American vocal groups like the Platters and the Moonglows reached white teens through disc jockeys who refused to go along with racial exclusion, the most famous being Cleveland's Alan Freed.

In 1954, Brown versus Board of Education ordered public schools to integrate, and the book gives rock, which grew from both African American and white music, part of the credit for relaxing racist attitudes.
Here are the Platters.
Only You, by The Platters. Doo-wop, 1955.
To recap chapter one.
From West African traditions, the blues took polyrhythm, blue notes, and call and response.
From European traditions, it took the regular four beat bar, the A A B lyric scheme, and the twelve bar chord progression.
As recording technology spread, blues musicians moved to cities and played with jazz bands and their instruments.

Rock grew out of the many styles of the forties, became a style of its own in the early fifties, depended on recording technology more than any style before it, and helped move America toward integration and mutual respect.
End of chapter one.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.sub: Urban Blues and Rhythm and Blues

n: Before chapter two, the book introduces the decade of the fifties.
In 1950, Americans feared the communist Soviet Union and People's Republic of China, especially since the Soviets had already tested an atomic bomb.
Families who could afford it built bomb shelters, and schools ran drills where children hid under their desks.

Fear of communism at home led to the execution of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg in 1953, and to Senator Joseph McCarthy's investigations, and the House Un-American Activities Committee's blacklist destroyed many Hollywood careers.
Still, the fifties were prosperous for most white middle class Americans.
The baby boom generation was born, and parents gave their children more freedom and money, so for the first time teenagers' tastes decided what was popular.

Part of that youth culture was the image of the rebellious antihero, created by movies: The Wild One, with Marlon Brando as a motorcycle gang leader, Blackboard Jungle, and James Dean's Rebel Without a Cause.
Rockabilly singers such as Gene Vincent and Eddie Cochran wore the black leather jackets of that image, but the book stresses that the movies created the image, not the rock artists.
For African Americans, the fifties were a time of recognizing their unequal status and deciding together to change it.

In 1954, Brown versus Board of Education ordered segregated schools to integrate, and in 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, starting the bus boycott led by Doctor Martin Luther King Junior.
Entertainment was segregated too: at New York's Cotton Club, Duke Ellington and other jazz greats played to white audiences only.
By the fifties, some clubs had separate black nights and white nights, or roped off the dance floor.
As white teenagers came to love rhythm and blues, they rejected that segregation, and the ropes came down.
As Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.) said at the time, what's happening, salt and pepper all mixed together.
In many ways, rock was a music of integration.
Johnny B. Goode, by Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.). Rock and roll, 1958.
Chapter two: Urban Blues and Rhythm and Blues.
The point of this chapter is how the blues moved to the city, where the guitar became a solo instrument, and how rhythm and blues added the energy and the backbeat that rock would keep.
The blues grew out of slavery and the rejection African Americans still faced after freedom, but it was not always sad music: it helped people cope, and many lyrics looked forward to better times.

During World War One, boll weevils destroyed the cotton crops of the Mississippi delta while northern factories needed workers, so many southern African Americans moved to cities like Chicago, Kansas City, and New York.
Musicians trained in country blues began playing together in groups instead of alone, and a new style developed: urban blues.
Urban blues groups had a rhythm section of bass, drums, guitar, or piano, plus solo instruments like the saxophone, and the band answered the singer's lines and played instrumental choruses.
An unamplified guitar couldn't be heard over a band, so it mostly strummed rhythm, until the electric guitar arrived.
T-Bone Walker (T-Bone. Walker.), 1910 to 1975, was one of the first musicians to use the electric guitar as a solo blues instrument.
He grew up in Texas playing country blues in the style of Blind Lemon Jefferson, then developed a flashy solo style of highly embellished melodies, and played the guitar behind his back on stage.
He strongly influenced the blues guitarist B.B. King and the rock guitarist Chuck Berry.
Call It Stormy Monday, by T-Bone Walker (T-Bone. Walker.). Urban blues, 1947.
Three O'Clock Blues, by B.B. King, 1951.
Urban blues.
King was a Mississippi born guitarist whose expressive solo style influenced Eric Clapton, Jimi Hendrix, and many other rock guitarists.
Listen for his guitar fills answering and imitating his singing, bending strings to reach blue notes, over soft, sustained saxophone chords.
items.lyr: It's three o'clock in the morning and he can't sleep, because the woman he loves has left him. He's so low that he talks about ending it all, and says goodbye to everyone. "Three o'clock in the morning" is a classic blues image of the loneliest, sleepless hour.
nl: B.B. King (B.B. King.), 1925 to 2015, came from Mississippi, the home of the delta blues.
B.B. came from his nickname, Blues Boy, and his real name was Riley B. King.
The listening guide is Three O'Clock Blues, from 1951, number one on the rhythm and blues charts for five weeks.

It's a slow twelve bar blues, at about 76 beats per minute, in which King sings and then answers each vocal line with his guitar, imitating and expanding the melody, and bending strings to reach blue notes.
Saxophones accompany with long held chords, and the drums are very soft, with little accent on the backbeat.
A touch of urban sophistication is the half step slide into some of the chords.
In the lyrics, he wakes in the early morning to find his lover gone, and the local pool hall may be his only comfort.
Compared to the rhythmic freedom of Robert Johnson, the regular beat and structure here show the urbanization of the blues, and King's guitar lines are as important as the lines he sings.
King once said that when he plays, he can hear himself singing.
Three O'Clock Blues, by B.B. King (B.B. King.). Urban blues, 1951.

n: King played with groups of every size and with orchestras, and in 1988 he appeared with U2 in their movie Rattle and Hum, asking their guitarist to take care of the chords so he could play melodic lines.
On his 1993 album Blues Summit, he played duets with John Lee Hooker, Lowell Fulson, and Robert Cray.
His lyrical, expressive style influenced many rock guitarists, including Eric Clapton, Jimmy Page, Jimi Hendrix, and Mike Bloomfield.
Clapton said he didn't think there was a better blues guitarist in the world than B.B. King.
Here they are together.
Riding with the King, by Eric Clapton & B.B. King. Blues rock, 2000.
Chicago drew many African American workers during both world wars, and Chicago musicians formed groups and switched to electric guitars.
Their style, called Chicago blues, combined swing jazz and boogie woogie piano with the passion of the delta blues.
Much of the credit goes to Chess Records, run by the brothers Phil and Leonard Chess, immigrants from Poland, which gave rural players backup bands and amplification that made their sound urban.
Chess's songwriter, producer, and bass player Willie Dixon wrote many of its most famous songs, including Hoochie Coochie Man.
Not every blues sounding song follows the twelve bar form: some stay on a single chord and keep the blues feel through blue notes and uneven beat subdivisions.
Muddy Waters (Muddy. Waters.), from Rolling Fork, Mississippi, used his real name, McKinley Morganfield, as a songwriter, and legend says his nickname came from catching fish by hand in muddy water.
His early hits, like Rollin' Stone from 1948, were close to country blues, with the whining sound of a bottleneck guitar.
Rollin' Stone stays on one chord throughout, and gets its blues feel from bent blue notes and a relaxed, uneven beat.
Rollin' Stone, by Muddy Waters (Muddy. Waters.). Delta blues, 1950.
Hoochie Coochie Man, by Muddy Waters, 1954, written by Willie Dixon.
Chicago blues.
Waters was a Mississippi slide guitarist who went electric in Chicago and recorded for Chess Records.
Listen for the stop time riff, where the band plays a short pattern and then stops so his voice is alone, and for the extra long sixteen bar choruses.
items.lyr: A boast about having supernatural powers with women. A "hoochie coochie man" is a man full of sexual power (the hoochie coochie was an erotic dance). A gypsy fortune teller predicted his birth, and he carries good-luck charms from African American folk magic, called hoodoo: a "black cat bone," a "mojo" (a charm bag), and "John the Conqueroo" (a root carried for luck). He was born on the seventh hour of the seventh day of the seventh month, and seven is a magic number.
nl: When Muddy Waters switched to electric guitar and added a band, his sound changed from country blues to the urban blues he's best known for.
The listening guide is Willie Dixon's song, I'm Your Hoochie Coochie Man, recorded by Muddy Waters in 1954, which reached number three on the rhythm and blues charts but never made the pop charts.
Its vocal choruses have four extra bars in the first A section, making them sixteen bars, and each A section includes a two beat stop time, where the band briefly stops.
The drums keep an uneven beat with little backbeat, while the piano sometimes slips into even subdivisions, creating a polyrhythm against the drums.
The lyrics boast of supernatural sexual power, with a gypsy fortune teller, a mojo, and a birth on the seventh hour of the seventh day of the seventh month.
As Willie Dixon put it, most blues singers were singing sad blues, but Muddy gave his blues a little pep.
Hoochie Coochie Man, by Muddy Waters (Muddy. Waters.). Chicago blues, 1954.

n: Muddy Waters never actually played rock and roll, but he often performed at rock concerts, including the Band's farewell concert in 1976, filmed as The Last Waltz, and he toured with Eric Clapton in 1979.
He died in 1983, after more than forty years of performing the blues.
His band included Jimmy Rogers on guitar, his half brother Otis Spann on piano, and Little Walter on blues harp, which is the harmonica.
Here's Little Walter.
Juke, by Little Walter. Chicago blues, 1952.
Elmore James (Elmore. James.), 1918 to 1963, claimed he had played with Robert Johnson, who suggested he slide a metal pipe along the strings the way others used a bottleneck.
He moved from Mississippi to Chicago, where he was among the first delta musicians to work regularly with saxophone, piano, and drums, an early modernizer of the delta blues.
His groups sounded modern, but his own playing remained bottleneck country blues, as in his recording of Robert Johnson's I Believe I'll Dust My Broom.
Dust My Broom, by Elmore James (Elmore. James.). Chicago blues, 1951.
His slide style was copied by many rock guitarists, including Eric Clapton, Brian Jones of the Rolling Stones, Jeremy Spencer of Fleetwood Mac, Jimi Hendrix, and Duane Allman.
Here's Duane Allman, with the Allman Brothers Band.
Statesboro Blues, by The Allman Brothers Band. Blues rock, 1971.
Chester Arthur Burnett, Howlin' Wolf (Howlin'. Wolf.), 1910 to 1976, got his name from the wolf like growls and howls in his act.
He played guitar and harp, learning guitar from Robert Johnson's style and harmonica from the original Sonny Boy Williamson.
His aggressive, sometimes raunchy sound didn't suit the pop charts.
Some of his songs are twelve bar blues, but Smokestack Lightnin' is chanted over a single chord.
Smokestack Lightnin', by Howlin' Wolf (Howlin'. Wolf.). Chicago blues, 1956.
Howlin' Wolf's songs were recorded by many rock bands, including Cream, the Yardbirds, Led Zeppelin, the Doors, the Grateful Dead, and the Rolling Stones.
In 1972 he recorded The London Sessions with rock musicians who had begun their careers playing his music, including Eric Clapton and members of the Rolling Stones, and he died in 1976.
Here's one of those covers: Willie Dixon's Little Red Rooster, a traditional twelve bar blues, by the Rolling Stones.
Little Red Rooster, by The Rolling Stones. Blues rock, 1964.
John Lee Hooker (John. Lee. Hooker.), 1917 to 2001, was based in Detroit rather than Chicago, but toured with the Chicago bluesmen.
His dramatic, delta based guitar and deep, rich voice gave him a career of almost six decades.
His twelve bar blues Boom Boom uses a break, where the instruments stop during the vocal line and then answer on the following beats, an effective kind of call and response.
Boom Boom, by John Lee Hooker (John. Lee. Hooker.). Detroit blues, 1962.
Boom Boom became a rock hit for the British group the Animals in 1965, keeping the same breaks.
Hooker kept recording and touring into the nineties, and his 1988 album The Healer featured rock and blues guests such as Santana, Bonnie Raitt, and Robert Cray.
Here's the Animals' version.
Boom Boom, by The Animals. British blues rock, 1965.

items.h: Chess Records and the Billboard charts
n: After Leonard Chess died in 1969, the Chess company was sold, but its recordings are still being reissued.
The blues is one of the most important roots of rock, but the blues by itself is not rock.

A side note on charts: Billboard started its charts in 1940, and because neighborhoods and radio stations were segregated, it kept three: pop, for the largest, mostly white audience; hillbilly, now country; and race, now rhythm and blues, which reflected African American tastes.
Rhythm and blues was called race music until the end of the forties.
It was dance music that accented the second and fourth beats of each bar, the backbeat, while most other music accented the first and third.
The blues reflected the problems of African American life, but rhythm and blues expressed the enjoyment of life.
It was played by rehearsed groups with wild stage shows, where saxophone players swiveled their hips and rolled on the floor, and singers shouted their lyrics.
That energy and backbeat became the basis of fifties rock and roll, while the sexually suggestive lyrics contributed to the backlash against rock.
Louis Jordan (Louis. Jordan.), 1908 to 1975, played saxophone in big jazz bands before forming his own group, Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five.
He called his style jumpin' jive, and his group was known as a jump band, as popular with white audiences as with African Americans, loved for his humor as much as his music.
Caldonia, by Louis Jordan (Louis. Jordan.). Jump blues, 1945.
Jordan influenced Little Richard's jump blues, later tributes like Joe Jackson's album Jumpin' Jive, and white rock musicians such as Bill Haley, who imitated his shuffle beat in the early fifties.
Here's Bill Haley, whom we'll meet again in chapter four.
Crazy Man, Crazy, by Bill Haley & His Comets. Early rock and roll, 1953.
Bo Diddley, by Bo Diddley, 1955.
Rhythm and blues, and early rock.
Bo Diddley was a Chicago guitarist who called himself a rhythm fanatic and played the guitar like a drum.
Listen for the Bo Diddley beat, repeated on guitar, drums, and maracas the whole time over a single chord, with no chord changes at all.
items.lyr: Built on the old lullaby "Hush, Little Baby," where a parent promises a child gifts. Here the mythical Bo Diddley tries everything to win his "pretty baby": he buys her a diamond ring, and when that fails he turns to black magic ("mojo"). Despite all his effort, she won't have him.
nl: Bo Diddley (Bo. Diddley.), born Ellas Bates, 1928 to 2008, strummed his guitar in a constant, throbbing rhythm that sounded almost like drums.
He studied violin before switching to guitar, and the name Bo Diddley may come from the diddley bow, a one string instrument of African origin.
His music was considered rhythm and blues in the fifties, and his first record, Bo Diddley backed with I'm a Man, was number one on the rhythm and blues charts.
The listening guide is the song Bo Diddley, from 1955, at about 104 beats per minute.
It isn't in blues form: it stays on a single chord, in irregular phrases of seventeen, twenty four, and nineteen bars.
The maracas keep even subdivisions, and the rhythm known as the Bo Diddley beat repeats throughout, while between vocal sections he slides a bottleneck to suggest chord changes.
He didn't invent the beat, but it carries his name because he popularized it and played it with such energy.
In the lyrics, the mythical Bo Diddley tries everything, from a diamond ring to black magic, but his pretty baby still won't go for it.
He called himself a rhythm fanatic who played the guitar as if he were playing drums.
Bo Diddley, by Bo Diddley (Bo. Diddley.). Rhythm and blues, 1955.

n: British groups like the Yardbirds, the Rolling Stones, and the Animals covered his songs, and the Bo Diddley beat has been used in many rock songs, by artists from the Who and Bruce Springsteen to U2.
One of the first was Buddy Holly's Not Fade Away. Listen for the beat.
Not Fade Away, by Buddy Holly. Rock and roll, 1957.
One of the most important rhythm and blues pianists was Professor Longhair (Professor. Longhair.), Henry Roeland Byrd, 1918 to 1980, from New Orleans.
His rollicking boogie woogie bass lines were based on a piano style developed by African Americans in the South in the twenties, which became basic to most rock piano.

In boogie woogie, the left hand plays a fast repeated pattern of two notes per beat, doubling the basic beat for a driving effect, while the right hand plays short repeated bits of melody called riffs.
His Mardi Gras in New Orleans is still played every year as the carnival's theme song.
Mardi Gras in New Orleans, by Professor Longhair (Professor. Longhair.). New Orleans rhythm and blues, 1949.
Longhair influenced the rock styles of Huey Piano Smith, Dr. John, Allen Toussaint, and Fats Domino, whom we'll hear much more of in chapter four.
Here's Fats Domino's first hit.
The Fat Man, by Fats Domino. New Orleans rhythm and blues, 1949.
To recap chapter two.
In urban blues, the guitar moved from accompaniment to solo instrument, playing alongside piano, drums, and horns.
Chicago blues was urban blues heavily influenced by swing jazz and boogie woogie piano, and urban blues led directly to fifties rock guitar.
Rhythm and blues used blue notes but usually not the twelve bar form, and it was meant as lighthearted dance music rather than a reflection of hardship.
It was played from rehearsed arrangements, yet performed wildly and full of sexual innuendo, and both its sexuality and its backbeat became basic characteristics of rock.
End of chapter two.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.sub: Gospel and Country Roots of Rock

n: Chapter three: Gospel and Country Roots of Rock.
The point of this chapter is that the blues didn't become rock on its own: it had to combine with two other traditions.
Black gospel gave rock its way of singing, with a soloist improvising ornaments against a group, which led to doo-wop.
Country music gave rock its steady beat, simple harmonies, storytelling lyrics, and, through western swing and honky-tonk, the bands of early rock and roll.

Rock was created from both directions: musicians raised on blues and gospel, such as Fats Domino, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard, added country characteristics, while country trained musicians, such as Bill Haley, Elvis Presley, and Buddy Holly, added blue notes and uneven beat subdivisions.

items.s: Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen
n: The religious folk songs of the seventeen and eighteen hundreds were called spirituals, and over time the word came to mean the religious songs of African Americans.

They were passed on by memory rather than written down, and descriptions like the 1867 book Slave Songs of the United States report that lead singers improvised, sliding between notes and singing turns around the melody, while the others kept to the plain melody, a practice that later became common in black gospel.
Spirituals ranged from fast, energetic songs called jubilees to slow, sorrowful songs, such as Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen.
Nobody Knows the Trouble I've Seen, by Mahalia Jackson. Spiritual, traditional.
Spirituals often carried coded messages.
On the surface they celebrated reaching heaven, but underneath they told slaves how to escape to freedom in the North.

Wade in the Water sounded like a song about baptism, but it also told escaping slaves to travel through streams so their owners' dogs couldn't follow their scent, and the owners appear in the lyrics as a band of angels coming after me.
Wade in the Water, by The Fisk Jubilee Singers. Spiritual, traditional.
Black gospel grew from the same roots as the blues: West African scales and call and response, combined with European harmony, regular beats, and instruments like the guitar and piano.
The difference is that the blues expresses one person's feelings, while gospel expresses the shared beliefs of a group of worshipers.

Before the Civil War, slaves attended church with their owners and sang hymns the European way, with even beat subdivisions, a style called white gospel that shares many traditions with hillbilly music.

After the war, African Americans built their own churches and developed a style full of the energy of camp meetings and jubilee spirituals, where a lead singer sings the verses and a group answers with the refrain.

By the thirties, gospel meant the more sophisticated religious music of composers such as Lucie Campbell and Thomas A. Dorsey (Thomas. A. Dorsey.), whose best known song is Take My Hand, Precious Lord.
Take My Hand, Precious Lord, by Thomas A. Dorsey (Thomas. A. Dorsey.). Black gospel, 1932.

items.s: How Far Am I from Canaan?
n: How Far Am I from Canaan, by... the Soul Stirrers... with...  Sam Cooke... as singing lead, 1952.
Black gospel.
The... Soul Stirrers... were an influential Texas gospel group, and... SamCooke... later became a soul and pop star.
Listen for... Sam Cooke's melismas, sliding around notes, before landing on them, and for the moment the tempo doubles halfway through.
Soul Stirrers
With Sam Cooke
items.lyr: Canaan is the Promised Land in the Bible, used here to mean heaven. The singer longs to get there, to hear the angels singing, to see his mother again, and to meet his Savior. The repeated question, "how far am I," admits he still has struggles ahead before he arrives.
nl: In the next listening, we will listen to:
How Far Am I from Canaan, by... the Soul Stirrers... with... Sam Cooke... as singing lead... 1952... Black gospel...
Gospel singers improvised vocal devices that later became characteristic of soul music.
One is the turn, called a melisma in its more elaborate form, where the singer slides around the notes above and below a melody note before finally landing on it.
Another is breaking a single syllable into several parts with bursts of breath, to build intensity.
Church services also had energetic, syncopated rhythms, dancing in the aisles, clapping, and shouting, something many soul singers later made part of their stage act.
The Soul Stirrers

The Soul Stirrers... from Texas, influenced other gospel groups with falsetto lead singing, meaning higher than the normal tenor range and usually breathy, along with polyrhythms and improvised lyrics.
The listening guide is How Far Am I from Canaan, from 1952, with an eighteen year old... Sam Cooke... singing lead.
Halfway through, the tempo doubles from about 96 to about 192 beats per minute, which is called double time.
Sam Cooke... embellishes the melody with melismas throughout, while the group sustains chords or sings bits of the lyrics, but never improvises as much as he does.
The only instrument is the drums. the bass drum is on the beat and the hi hat is on the backbeats. The beat subdivisions are uneven.
Canaan, the Promised Land, stands for heaven, and the singer's question "how far am I?", and admits that he still has struggles ahead in this world.
How Far Am I from Canaan?
by
The Soul Stirrers
Black gospel

n: Both Sam Cooke and the Memphis soul singer Johnny Taylor began their careers in the Soul Stirrers.
Sam Cooke went on to become a rock singer and songwriter, popular in the late fifties and early sixties.
You Send Me, by Sam Cooke (Sam. Cooke.). Pop and rhythm and blues, 1957.
Oh Happy Day, by the Edwin Hawkins Singers, 1969.
Gospel, in a large choir style with a rock beat.
Edwin Hawkins was an Oakland pianist and arranger whose choir took gospel onto the pop charts.
Listen for soloist Dorothy Morrison's melismas against the choir's plainer answers, and the clapping on the backbeat.
items.lyr: Joy about the day the singer was converted to Christianity: Jesus "washed my sins away," an image of baptism. He also taught the singer to watch, fight, and pray, and to live rejoicing every day. In other words: being saved is a happy day, but life still takes effort.
nl: Female gospel groups became popular in the forties, and in 1961 the Clara Ward Singers left the church circuit to perform in Las Vegas, although many gospel performers were uneasy about taking gospel music out of church.

In the sixties, Edwin Hawkins (Edwin. Hawkins.), a pianist and arranger in Oakland, California, popularized a full choir style, accompanying his large choir with a rock beat on keyboards, bass, and drums, and his gospel songs became pop hits.
The listening guide is Oh Happy Day, from 1969, number four on the pop charts and number two on the rhythm and blues charts.

Soloist Dorothy Morrison uses the traditional gospel devices, especially melismas on the words oh and day, and because a large choir can't sing those devices, her improvisations stand out clearly against its plainer responses.
Near the end, a high female voice improvises above the choir, a sound later copied in disco.
The rhythm section keeps a steady tempo of about 112, with even subdivisions, while the singers gradually push ahead of it, creating a feeling of fervor.
The lyrics express joy at religious conversion, with washing as an image of baptism.
Oh Happy Day, by The Edwin Hawkins Singers (Edwin. Hawkins. Singers.). Gospel choir, 1969.

n: Gospel trained African American vocal groups were singing secular music as early as the twenties.
Their sound came to be called doo-wop, after the nonsense syllables, like ah or dum dum de dum, that backup singers sang behind or in response to the lead singer.
Two early groups shaped the doo-wop style.
The first was The Mills Brothers (Mills. Brothers.), with smooth, sophisticated four part harmony, and a bass singer who sang a moving line like a string bass.
Paper Doll, by The Mills Brothers (Mills. Brothers.). Vocal group pop, 1942.

The second was The Ink Spots (Ink. Spots.), whose high tenor lead often dropped out after a chorus so the bass singer could speak the lyrics while the others hummed chords. Listen for the spoken bass.
If I Didn't Care, by The Ink Spots (Ink. Spots.). Vocal group pop, 1939.
In 1945, the Ravens combined the mellow style of the Mills Brothers with the Ink Spots' lead bass, while their pianist played the constant triplet pattern that much later doo-wop would use.
Since doo-wop was mainly a vocal style, instruments stayed in the background.
The Ravens were copied by many groups, some of which also took bird names: the Crows, the Penguins, the Cardinals, and the Flamingos.
Here's one of them, the Penguins.
Earth Angel, by The Penguins. Doo-wop, 1954.
Another bird group, The Orioles (Orioles.) from Baltimore, built their sound on the light tenor lead of the Ink Spots.
Their 1953 recording of Crying in the Chapel was one of the first records by African American artists to succeed on the pop charts.
It was a cover, meaning a new recording of an existing song, of a country hit by the white singer Darrell Glenn.
To compare the white and black gospel styles, we'll hear Glenn's original first.
Crying in the Chapel, by Darrell Glenn. Country, 1953.
Crying in the Chapel, by the Orioles, 1953.
Doo-wop.
The Orioles were a Baltimore vocal group, and this cover of a country song was one of the first African American hits on the pop charts.
Listen for Sonny Til's gospel style turns in the lead, over the group's soft ahs and a shuffle beat with a strong backbeat.
items.lyr: Someone saw the singer crying in a small, plain chapel (a little church) and thought he was sad, but they were tears of joy. He searched everywhere for happiness and only found peace of mind by praying humbly. He tells the listener to take their troubles to the chapel too.
nl: The Orioles' version reached number eleven pop and was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for five weeks.

Comparing it to Glenn's shows the basic contrast: white gospel follows the steady beat and instruments of country music, while black gospel uses a shuffle rhythm, a backbeat, vocal improvisation, and a backup chorus.
In the listening guide, Sonny Til sings the lead with many turns and other gospel embellishments, while the other Orioles answer with ahs and words from the lyrics.
It's in A A B A song form, at about 69 beats per minute, with uneven subdivisions, a strong backbeat on the drums, and trumpet, alto sax, Hammond organ, and bass.
The lyrics contrast the spiritual peace of a plain and simple chapel with the emptiness of the outside world.
Elvis Presley later covered it in a style much closer to the Orioles' than to Glenn's.
Crying in the Chapel, by The Orioles (Orioles.). Doo-wop, 1953.

n: Sh-Boom, by the Chords, 1954.
Doo-wop.
The Chords were an African American vocal group from New York, and this is the original version of the song.
Listen for the solo bass singer on the bridge and the jazzy tenor saxophone solo, so you can compare them with the white cover that comes next.
items.lyr: A dreamy love song: life could be a dream, a paradise, if the singer could be with the one he loves and she would love him back. "Sh-boom" and the other sounds are nonsense syllables that imitate a heartbeat or simply sound happy. There is no deeper story.
nl: It was much more common for white groups to cover African American songs, often changing the lyrics, instruments, and production to sell better to white audiences.
A famous example is Sh-Boom, written and first recorded in 1954 by The Chords (Chords.), an African American group, and covered by the Crew-Cuts, a white group from Canada.
The Chords' version, at about 134 beats per minute, is accompanied by a small rhythm section of guitar, string bass, and drums, with a tenor saxophone taking a jazz style solo.
The bridge is sung by a solo bass singer, showing the Ink Spots' influence, and the beat subdivisions are uneven.
It reached number two on the rhythm and blues charts and the top ten on the pop charts.
Sh-Boom, by The Chords (Chords.). Doo-wop, 1954, the original.

n: Sh-Boom, by the Crew-Cuts, 1954.
A pop cover of the Chords' doo-wop hit.
The Crew-Cuts were a white group from Canada, and their version outsold the original, hitting number one for seven weeks.
Listen for the full swing band, the kettledrum, and the dramatic pauses, and notice that the bass solo and the sax solo are gone.
items.lyr: Same lyrics as the Chords' version: life could be a dream if he could be with his love. Only the nonsense syllables change, to more "sh-boom" and "la la la."
nl: The Crew-Cuts (Crew-Cuts.) kept the lyrics, except for the nonsense syllables, but whitened the sound, replacing the small band with a full swing dance band and kettledrum, using no bass soloist, and dropping the instrumental solo.
As often happened, the cover outsold the original, and the Crew-Cuts were number one on the pop charts for seven weeks.
Sh-Boom also uses the chord progression found in so many doo-wop songs that it's called the doo-wop progression: one, six minor seven, two minor seven, five seven.
Doo-wop accompaniments also pound out repeated chords three to a beat, a triplet pattern that the bass and melody follow.
Sh-Boom, by The Crew-Cuts (Crew-Cuts.). Pop cover, 1954.

n: The book explains how cover records work.

Songwriters control the first recording of their songs, but after that anyone may record a cover, and as long as the cover credits the original writer, the writer can't stop it, though the writer does collect the royalties.

In the early nineties, a publisher sued the rap group 2 Live Crew over their parody of Roy Orbison's Oh, Pretty Woman, but the Supreme Court ruled for 2 Live Crew, because they had the right to parody it.
Since 1978, copyright lasts the writer's life plus seventy years, after which the song enters the public domain and anyone can use it without paying royalties.
There Goes My Baby, by the Drifters, 1959.
Rhythm and blues vocal group, with Ben E. King singing lead.
This was the first rhythm and blues record with a full orchestral string section, produced by Leiber and Stoller.
Listen for the swirling violins and booming kettledrums behind the voices, with no backbeat.
items.lyr: He watches the woman he loves walk away. She left without saying why, and he wonders whether she loves him and whether she'll come back. He regrets that he never told her how much he loved her.
nl: Back to doo-wop.
The Drifters (Drifters.) got their name because members drifted from group to group, and not a single member stayed for the group's whole career.
In the fifties they added a Latin beat to some songs and copied the lead bass of the Ink Spots and the Ravens.
The original Drifters broke up in 1958, but their manager owned the name and gave it to a group called the Five Crowns, with Ben E. King singing lead.
The new Drifters reached number two pop and number one rhythm and blues with There Goes My Baby, written and produced by Leiber and Stoller.
It was the first rhythm and blues record with a full orchestral string background, which became a trend in the early sixties, though Buddy Holly had already used strings on his last hit.

In the listening guide, strings and kettledrums provide most of the accompaniment, with no accented backbeat, and the chords are a variant of the doo-wop progression in which each chord lasts two bars.
The lyrics: his baby has left him brokenhearted without saying why, and he wishes he could tell her he loves her.
There Goes My Baby, by The Drifters (Drifters.). Rhythm and blues, 1959.

items.s: In the Still of the Nite
n: Many other doo-wop groups had hits in the fifties, including the Moonglows, the Coasters, the Five Satins, the Rays, and the Clovers, and groups named after cars, such as the Cadillacs, the Impalas, the Fleetwoods, and the Edsels.

They all drew mainly on the Mills Brothers, the Ink Spots, the Ravens, and the Orioles, and their style was smoothly romantic, moderately slow, and danceable, with lead singers using gospel devices like breath punctuations and embellished phrase endings.
Here's one of them, the Five Satins.
In the Still of the Nite, by The Five Satins. Doo-wop, 1956.
From the late fifties through the early seventies, smooth doo-wop gave way to gutsier African American styles called soul.
The word soul first described gospel groups' power to stir people's souls, but by the early sixties it meant secular music made mostly by and for African Americans, expressing African American pride.
Gospel and doo-wop became very popular again in the nineties, with singers and groups such as Amy Grant, Take 6, All-4-One, and Boyz II Men.
Here's Boyz II Men.
End of the Road, by Boyz II Men. Rhythm and blues, 1992.
Now the second root: country music.
Country music is a commercial form of folk music, first called hillbilly, after the backwoods southerners of British descent who played it.

Settlers from the British Isles brought dances like the jig, reel, polka, and waltz, along with hymns and ballads, to the southern mountains, played on the fiddle, guitar, dulcimer, and banjo, which African Americans had developed from an African instrument called the banza.
As songwriter Harlan Howard put it, country music is three chords and the truth.
In the twenties, radio barn dance shows brought it to the rest of the country, and the WSM Barn Dance, first broadcast in 1925, was renamed the Grand Ole Opry.
Here's what to listen for in the country music that influenced rock.
The beat is crisp and exact, with every musician playing right on it, and beats are divided evenly, giving a boom chunk feel.
Harmonies are usually simple triads, three note chords without added sevenths, and most songs repeat eight bar periods made of two four bar phrases.
The bass often plays the root of the chord on beat one and the fifth on beat three, which is called two beat bass.
Lyrics tell stories or express feelings and are meant to be heard clearly over the accompaniment.
Vocals are often nasal, sung deadpan or as if on the verge of tears, and voices and instruments often slide from note to note, and the steel guitar can bend entire chords.
In the thirties and forties, a style called western swing became popular in Texas.

It grew out of fiddle and guitar barn dance bands that adopted the blues and jazz: from the blues, it took the twelve bar form and blue notes, from jazz, syncopation, saxophones, and improvised solos, and from both, uneven beat subdivisions and the backbeat.
It was also one of the few hillbilly styles to use drums, which most country styles avoided, partly because of their association with African American music.
The king of western swing was the fiddler Bob Wills (Bob. Wills.), 1905 to 1975, who led the Texas Playboys.
Western swing, and another blues influenced country style called hillbilly boogie, became important to rock and roll through the music of Bill Haley.
San Antonio Rose, by Bob Wills & His Texas Playboys (Bob. Wills. &. His. Texas. Playboys.). Western swing, 1938.

A honky-tonk was a loud, rowdy bar, often just outside the limits of dry towns, so the music had to be amplified and have a steady, danceable beat, with pianists playing rollicking boogie woogie bass patterns.
Honky-tonk songs were often about losing a job or an untrue lover.
The amplified guitar, bass, and drums of honky-tonk influenced the rockabilly of Elvis Presley, Eddie Cochran, and Gene Vincent, and Jerry Lee Lewis took his piano style from honky-tonk pianists.
Popular honky-tonk singers included George Jones, Hank Williams, whom we'll hear soon, and Ernest Tubb (Ernest. Tubb.), known as the Texas Troubadour.
Walking the Floor Over You, by Ernest Tubb (Ernest. Tubb.). Honky-tonk, 1941.
Jimmie Rodgers (Jimmie. Rodgers.), 1897 to 1933, is often called the Father of Country Music.

His distinctive vocal style was called blue yodeling, rapidly switching between high and low notes, and the word blue refers to the many twelve bar blues he sang, combining black and white styles as early as the twenties.
He also recorded newly written songs instead of mostly old ones, which led directly to the songwriting of Hank Williams, Johnny Cash, and other country artists.
Blue Yodel No. 1 (T for Texas), by Jimmie Rodgers (Jimmie. Rodgers.). Country, 1927.

items.s: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive
n: I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive, by Hank Williams, 1952.
Honky-tonk country.
Williams was one of country's greatest songwriters, and this was his last single before he died at twenty nine.
Listen for the steel guitar and fiddles sliding between notes, the two beat bass, and his nasal voice with its little crying hiccups.
items.lyr: A comic list of bad luck: his fishing pole breaks, his rich uncle's will leaves him nothing, his shoes are worn out, and everything goes wrong. "I'll never get out of this world alive" is a joke: nobody does. He decides not to worry, since nothing will work out anyway. It became sadly ironic when he died months later.
nl: Hank Williams (Hank. Williams.), 1923 to 1953, recorded I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive when he was twenty eight, and it became a number one country hit and his last single.
A dependency on painkillers and alcohol led to his death by heart attack a year later.
In the listening guide, at about 118 beats per minute, the beat is steady, but uneven subdivisions give it a western swing feel.

The string bass plays two beat bass, the acoustic guitar accents the backbeats, and a steel guitar and two fiddles take turns in the instrumental sections, sliding between notes, while the drums are barely there.
The harmonies are simple triads, and Williams's nasal voice adds hiccup like slides that make him sound close to tears.
The lyrics are a classic country bad luck lament, in which the singer can't win for losing.
I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive, by Hank Williams (Hank. Williams.). Honky-tonk country, 1952.

n: I Walk the Line, by Johnny Cash, 1956.
Country, from Sun Records, the same label as Elvis.
Cash, known as the Man in Black, crossed over from the country charts to the pop charts with this song.
Listen for the muffled boom chicka guitar, made by weaving wax paper through the strings, and the two beat bass.
items.lyr: A promise of faithfulness. "Walking the line" means staying on the right path and behaving yourself, and here it means staying true to the woman he loves. He keeps a close watch on his heart and keeps his eyes wide open, meaning he won't be tempted by anyone else while they're apart.
nl: Johnny Cash (Johnny. Cash.), 1932 to 2003, became a country star just as rock was becoming popular.
He auditioned at Sun Records, where Elvis was already recording, and released Cry, Cry, Cry and Folsom Prison Blues, both country hits.
In 1956, he crossed over to the pop charts with I Walk the Line, number one country for six weeks and number seventeen pop.
In the listening guide, every verse uses the same melody, which is called strophic form.
The beat is divided evenly, both the bass and the guitar play two beat bass, the drums are barely audible, and Cash wove wax paper through his guitar strings for a muffled sound.
The song is a tribute to fidelity, with walking the line meaning staying true.
I Walk the Line, by Johnny Cash (Johnny. Cash.). Country, 1956.

n: Cash's biggest pop hit was A Boy Named Sue, in 1969, and while other country stars wore sparkling outfits, he dressed in black and became known as the Man in Black.
He sang with Bob Dylan, and later worked with the producer Rick Rubin, known for rap and metal, who saw Cash as rock's original dark outsider.
In 2003, the year he died, Cash covered Nine Inch Nails' song Hurt, saying it had more heart, soul, and pain than any song he'd heard in a long time.
Hurt, by Johnny Cash (Johnny. Cash.). Country, 2002.
To recap chapter three.

Like the blues, black gospel came from both African and European traditions, but it was religious music sung by groups to share their beliefs, with soloists improvising ornaments that the choir did not.
Groups like the Mills Brothers and the Ink Spots made secular versions of gospel groups, and their imitators created doo-wop, which was revived in the nineties.

Country music, called hillbilly until the early fifties, is commercial folk music, with a steady, evenly divided beat, simple triads, eight bar periods, two beat bass, sliding between notes, and vocals that are never covered by the instruments.
Western swing and hillbilly boogie were the basis of Bill Haley's early rock, honky-tonk combined with the blues created rockabilly, and bluegrass later shaped country rock.
End of chapter three.
Chapter four: Early Rock and Roll.
The point of this chapter is that rock and roll came together from two directions in the fifties.
First, African American musicians from rhythm and blues and gospel, Fats Domino, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard, who added country and pop influences.
Second, white country musicians, Bill Haley, Elvis Presley, Carl Perkins, Jerry Lee Lewis, and Buddy Holly, who covered and absorbed the blues, creating rockabilly.

When the disc jockey Alan Freed first used the term rock and roll, he meant rhythm and blues, and the exact point where rock begins can't be found, but by the fifties these styles were definitely rock.
Fats Domino (Fats. Domino.), 1929 to 2017, whose real name was Antoine Domino, was born in New Orleans, a center for jazz since before nineteen hundred.
His producer and co-writer, the bandleader Dave Bartholomew, backed Domino's friendly, understated voice with honking saxophones.
Domino had several rhythm and blues hits before reaching the pop charts in 1955 with Ain't That a Shame, crossing over to white audiences.
Ain't That a Shame, by Fats Domino (Fats. Domino.). Rhythm and blues, 1955.
I'm Walkin', by Fats Domino, 1956.
New Orleans rhythm and blues and rock and roll.
Domino was a pianist and singer from New Orleans whose friendly voice was popular with both white and African American audiences.
Listen for the hand claps on the backbeat, the shuffle rhythm, and the growling tenor saxophone solo.
items.lyr: He's walking and talking, hoping his baby will come back to him. He's lonely, and he's going to keep walking until she returns. "Walking" stands for his effort to win her back.
nl: Domino could sing slow, smooth songs like Blueberry Hill as well as rollicking boogie woogie like I'm Walkin', both from 1956.
I'm Walkin' was his eighth number one rhythm and blues hit, staying there for six weeks, and it reached number four on the pop charts.
In the listening guide, it's in A A B A form at a fast tempo of about 224, with a shuffle beat.
The introduction has drum thumps on beats one and three and hand claps on the backbeats, two and four, which continue through the song.
The bass and guitar repeat a two bar pattern together, and a growling tenor saxophone improvises around the vocal melody.
Walking stands for the singer's attempt to get his girl back.
Domino placed thirty seven records in the top forty by 1963.
I'm Walkin', by Fats Domino (Fats. Domino.). New Orleans rock and roll, 1956.

n: Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.), 1926 to 2017, was a guitarist and singer rooted in blues and rhythm and blues, but his music was unquestionably rock and roll.

Born in Saint Louis, he took his guitar style from T-Bone Walker and Muddy Waters, but his singing clearly showed the influence of white country and western singers, and that fusion of blues and country roots made his sound rock and roll.
He even defined rock's style and its essential backbeat, in both his playing and his lyrics, in his 1957 hit Rock and Roll Music.
Rock and Roll Music, by Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.). Rock and roll, 1957.
Berry wrote most of his own material, and his lyrics captured the teenage spirit.
In Roll Over Beethoven, he tells classical composers to roll over in their graves, and in his first hit, Maybellene, from 1955, his V8 Ford catches up with a Cadillac Coupe de Ville.
Maybellene, by Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.). Rock and roll, 1955.

items.s: School Day (Ring! Ring! Goes the Bell)
n: School Day, by Chuck Berry, 1957.
Rock and roll.
Berry was a guitarist, singer, and songwriter from Saint Louis, often called the Father of Rock Guitar.
Listen for the breaks at the end of each chorus, where the band stops and he sings alone, and for his guitar answering each vocal line.
items.lyr: A teenager's school day from start to finish: getting up early, a hard teacher, a crowded lunch, and the clock dragging. At three o'clock the bell rings and he runs to the local "juke joint" (a hangout with a jukebox), drops a coin in the slot, and dances. The closing lines hail rock and roll as a release from the old, boring ways of the adult world.
nl: In School Day, from 1957, dancing to rock and roll is what gets you through a day at school.
His performances were electrifying, and included his famous duckwalk, crossing the stage with his knees bent and his head moving back and forth.
In his solos, he would take a short riff and dig into it harder with each repetition, a sound that became standard rock guitar.
School Day reached number three pop and was number one rhythm and blues for five weeks.
In the listening guide, it's a twelve bar blues at about 148 beats per minute, with a shuffle beat.
Each chorus except the instrumental one ends with a three beat break, where the band stops and the voice leads into the next chorus, and the guitar fills often imitate the vocal line they answer.
Behind it all, the piano plays a slower triplet pattern, half the speed of the guitar and drums, called a hemiola, easiest to hear behind the guitar solo.
School Day (Ring! Ring! Goes the Bell), by Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.). Rock and roll, 1957.

n: Late in 1959, Berry was charged under the Mann Act, for transporting an underage woman across a state line, and he was in prison from early 1962 to early 1964.
When he came back, he picked up right where he had left off, with No Particular Place to Go, strikingly similar to School Day.

Berry is sometimes called the Father of Rock Guitar, because so many guitarists copied his style, including Buddy Holly, George Harrison of the Beatles, Keith Richards of the Rolling Stones, and Carl Wilson of the Beach Boys.
Here's Keith Richards, with the Rolling Stones, playing a Berry song.
Carol, by The Rolling Stones. Rock, 1964.
Richard Penniman, known as Little Richard (Little. Richard.), 1932 to 2020, was born in Macon, Georgia.
He learned piano in church, where he also sang gospel and learned its vocal slides and embellishments, which he combined with the shrieks and moans of his jump blues influenced rock.
His piano usually had a boogie woogie bass with chords pounded out above it, and what set him apart were his fast tempos and high energy.
Sex was his favorite subject, and he teased audiences with an androgynous hairstyle and heavy makeup while singing shockingly suggestive lyrics.
He wrote or co-wrote, sang, and played piano on hits including Tutti Frutti, Long Tall Sally, and Good Golly, Miss Molly, recorded in 1957.
Good Golly, Miss Molly, by Little Richard (Little. Richard.). Rock and roll, 1958.
Long Tall Sally, by Little Richard, 1956.
Rock and roll, with roots in jump blues and gospel.
Little Richard was a pianist and singer from Macon, Georgia, famous for his wild energy, shrieks, and flamboyant image.
Listen for the stop time, where the band hits single chords and drops out so his voice is alone, and the pounding piano.
items.lyr: Gossip played for laughs. He's going to tell Aunt Mary that Uncle John was out with "Long Tall Sally," a tall, flashy woman. When Uncle John sees Aunt Mary coming, he ducks back into the alley to hide. The singer wants to have some fun with Sally himself tonight. "Built for speed" means she's fast and exciting.
nl: Long Tall Sally was his biggest hit, reaching number six pop despite being banned in some cities, and number one rhythm and blues for eight weeks.
In the listening guide, it's a twelve bar blues at about 176 beats per minute, with the piano in a shuffle pattern and a saxophone solo in the middle.
Several choruses begin with stop time: the band plays a single chord on the first beat of three bars, then drops out, so the voice is heard alone.
Stop time differs from a full break, like the ones in Chuck Berry's School Day, because the instruments keep punctuating the vocal line with short chords.
In the lyrics, the singer has caught Uncle John with a loose woman, and hopes to have a chance with her himself that night.
Long Tall Sally, by Little Richard (Little. Richard.). Rock and roll, 1956.

n: In 1957, at the height of his success, Little Richard quit rock and roll to become a preacher.
He returned in 1986 with what he called message music, trading his androgynous image for that of a dancing preacher.
In 1962, in England, he shared a bill with the Beatles, who covered his hits, with Paul McCartney imitating his vocal style.
Now to rock musicians with a country background.
Bill Haley (Bill. Haley.), 1925 to 1981, was a country singer and guitarist from Michigan who played in western swing bands.
In 1951, his band, the Saddlemen, covered Rocket 88, a blues record by Jackie Brenston with Ike Turner's Kings of Rhythm.

Performing it showed Haley how much white teenagers loved the beat and vitality of the blues, so in 1952 he dropped his country image, renamed the group the Comets, and began recording blues and rhythm and blues.
Here's the original Rocket 88.
Rocket 88, by Jackie Brenston & His Delta Cats. Rhythm and blues, 1951.
Shake, Rattle and Roll, by Joe Turner, 1954.
Jump blues, or rhythm and blues.
Turner was a blues shouter from Kansas City who sang over honking saxophones.
Listen for the boogie woogie piano, the hand claps on the backbeat, and the jazzy baritone sax solo, so you can compare it with Bill Haley's cover next.
items.lyr: A man complains to his woman: she stays in bed instead of cooking, wears revealing dresses, and spends his money. Much of it is sexual double meaning: "shake, rattle and roll" means both dancing and sex, and "a one-eyed cat peeping in a seafood store" is a deliberately rude joke. That's why Bill Haley's cover changed many lines.
nl: In 1954, Bill Haley and the Comets signed with Decca and covered two blues songs: Rock Around the Clock, and Joe Turner's Shake, Rattle and Roll.
Joe Turner (Joe. Turner.), 1911 to 1985, had sung jazz since the late twenties, and was called a blues shouter, because he matched his voice to the honking saxophones.
In his own words, he put swing to the blues and made the blues jump.

His Shake, Rattle and Roll, from 1954, is a twelve bar blues at about 140 beats per minute, with boogie woogie piano, a bass on all four beats, hand claps and snare drum accenting the backbeats, and a jazz style baritone sax solo.
His lyrics are full of sexual references, like the couple being in bed together and the sun shining through her dress.
It was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for three weeks, but never made the pop charts.
Shake, Rattle and Roll, by Joe Turner (Joe. Turner.). Jump blues, 1954, the original.

n: Shake, Rattle and Roll, by Bill Haley and His Comets, 1954.
Rock and roll, from a former western swing bandleader.
Haley's version is faster and cleaned up for white radio audiences.
Listen for the slapped country bass, and the saxophone and guitar playing the riff together instead of a jazz solo.
items.lyr: The same basic complaint, but the sexual lines are removed: instead of being in bed, she's told to get out of the kitchen, and instead of revealing dresses she's cold and treats him wrong. The "one-eyed cat" line stayed, probably because most listeners wouldn't catch the joke.
nl: Haley's version is faster, at about 176, with fewer jazz characteristics.
The piano and drums play a shuffle, the bassist slaps the strings against the fingerboard in the country style, and the backbeat is less obvious.
Instead of an improvised solo, the sax and guitar play the melody together.
The references to the bed are removed, and the lines about her sexuality are changed to lines about her being cold and treating him wrong.
Haley's version reached number seven on the pop charts.
Shake, Rattle and Roll, by Bill Haley & His Comets (Bill. Haley. &. His. Comets.). Rock and roll, 1954, the cover.

n: Rock Around the Clock was number one on the pop charts for eight weeks.

It's a twelve bar blues with saxophones playing riffs rather than jazz improvisations, and its lyrics use the word rock to mean dancing and partying, though young listeners knew the blues singers' use of rock as slang for sex.
It became a hit after it was used in the 1955 movie Blackboard Jungle, about teen rebellion, so the thirty year old Haley came to stand for that attitude.
Haley's mix of western swing and rhythm and blues proved less lasting than rockabilly, the combination of honky-tonk country and rhythm and blues.
Rock Around the Clock, by Bill Haley & His Comets (Bill. Haley. &. His. Comets.). Rock and roll, 1954.

Sam Phillips (Sam. Phillips.), 1923 to 2003, moved to Memphis and opened the Memphis Recording Service, recording mostly African American blues musicians from the South, including Rocket 88, Howlin' Wolf, Rufus Thomas, and Junior Parker, and then formed the Sun Record Company to release them himself.
Phillips knew white teenagers loved rhythm and blues but tended to buy records by white artists, and that radio wanted sexual references kept out of lyrics.
He needed a white singer who could capture the style and beat of African American singers while adapting the lyrics to white tastes.
He found him in 1954, when the young Elvis Presley (Elvis. Presley.), 1935 to 1977, came into the studio to record a song as a birthday present for his mother.
Elvis's Sun recordings introduced American teenagers to rockabilly, a name made from rock and hillbilly.
The band was just an electric lead guitar, an acoustic rhythm guitar, a string bass, and subdued drums.

Guitarist Scotty Moore slid notes up the strings to imitate a steel guitar, bassist Bill Black slapped the strings against the fingerboard, a sound typical of rockabilly, and Phillips added reverberation that exaggerated the throbbing pulse.
Elvis's first single put a blues song on one side, That's All Right, by Arthur Big Boy Crudup.
That's All Right, by Elvis Presley (Elvis. Presley.). Rockabilly, 1954.
The other side was a rockabilly version of the country song Blue Moon of Kentucky, by the bluegrass writer Bill Monroe.
Phillips sent Elvis to audition for the Grand Ole Opry, but he was rejected, because his style was too black for the Opry and too white for rhythm and blues audiences.
His voice had no direct precedent: a wide, syrupy vibrato suggesting warmth, which could suddenly shift into a falsetto suggesting tension and wildness.
Blue Moon of Kentucky, by Elvis Presley (Elvis. Presley.). Rockabilly, 1954.
His Sun recordings follow the twelve bar blues form, but at faster tempos than blues or rhythm and blues, and that speed gave rockabilly its energy.
After his recording of Junior Parker's Mystery Train drew attention, his manager, Colonel Tom Parker, sold his contract to RCA for thirty five thousand dollars.

At RCA, Elvis became a star within a year, recording songs by pop writers with a clean studio sound and doo-wop style backup vocals, and his performance style earned him the title King of Rock and Roll.
In 1956, he sang Hound Dog and other hits on national TV, thrilling teenage girls and angering their parents, and Ed Sullivan showed him only from the waist up.
Hound Dog, by Willie Mae Big Mama Thornton, 1952, written by Leiber and Stoller.
Rhythm and blues.
Thornton was a powerful blues singer, and her version was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for seven weeks.
Listen for her rough, commanding voice, the bluesy guitar bending notes, and the very strong backbeat from claps and drums.
items.lyr: A woman throws out a man who has been cheating on her and living off her. In African American slang, a "hound dog" is a man who chases other women. "Wag your tail" mocks him like a begging dog; she's done feeding him.
nl: Hound Dog was written by the songwriting team of Leiber and Stoller for Willie Mae Big Mama Thornton (Big. Mama. Thornton.), who recorded it first, in 1952.
In African American slang, a hound dog was a man who cheated on his woman, and Thornton sings it to such a man, vowing to stop seeing him.

In the listening guide, her version is a twelve bar blues at about 140, sung in a rough classic blues voice, with country blues guitar fills bending into blue notes, and hand claps plus a drum hit on its shell for a very strong backbeat.
It was number one on the rhythm and blues charts for seven weeks, but never made the pop charts.
Hound Dog, by Big Mama Thornton (Big. Mama. Thornton.). Rhythm and blues, 1952, the original.

n: Hound Dog, by Elvis Presley, 1956.
Rock and roll.
Elvis's version was number one on the pop charts for eleven weeks, and it changes the meaning of Thornton's song.
Listen for the faster tempo, the drum hits on the backbeat, the country style guitar solo, and the backup singers holding long chords.
items.lyr: The lyrics were changed: now it's a man insulting someone as worthless, like a hound dog that "ain't never caught a rabbit," a useless hunting dog. "You ain't no friend of mine" and claims of being "high-classed" become lies he sees through. The cheating-man meaning of the original is gone.
nl: Elvis's 1956 version changes the meaning, berating a woman as no more useful than a hound dog that can't catch rabbits, which fit his tough guy image.
It's faster, starting at about 176 and speeding up, with country style guitar, drums heavily accenting the backbeat, and backup singers sustaining chords.
Backed with Don't Be Cruel, it was number one on the pop charts for eleven weeks and on the rhythm and blues charts for six.
Hound Dog, by Elvis Presley (Elvis. Presley.). Rock and roll, 1956, the cover.

n: Burning Love, by Elvis Presley, 1972.
Rock.
This was Elvis's last top ten hit, from his later career.
Listen for the strong backbeat, the mix of straight and swung rhythms, and the backup singers breaking into black gospel style at the end.
items.lyr: He's so full of love and desire that he feels like he's on fire: burning, his temperature rising, flames licking at his body. "A hunk, a hunk of burning love" means a big piece of passion. It's playful exaggeration, not a story.
nl: Elvis became a movie star, and in 1958 he was drafted into the army, where he served two years, and soon after his mother died, which he called the worst loss of his life.
After the army, he was more a movie star than a concert performer, until he returned to touring and Las Vegas shows from 1968 on.
His ability to follow trends kept him popular for three decades, and Buddy Holly once said that without Elvis, none of them could have made it.
The listening guide is his last top ten hit, Burning Love, from 1972, which reached number two on the pop charts.
At about 144 beats per minute, it mixes even and uneven subdivisions, with a strong backbeat on the drums and a backup group that breaks into black gospel style at the end.
The lyrics: he's so full of desire that he's burning up.
His dependence on prescription drugs contributed to his death in 1977, at forty two.
Burning Love, by Elvis Presley (Elvis. Presley.). Rock, 1972.

n: Blue Suede Shoes, by Carl Perkins, 1956.
Rockabilly.
Perkins was a Tennessee singer, guitarist, and songwriter at Sun Records, and this song was number one on the country charts and number two on pop and rhythm and blues.
Listen for the stop time openings, where his voice is alone except for hits on the beat, the slapped bass, and the drummer playing on the rim.
items.lyr: You can do anything to me: knock me down, burn my house, steal my car, drink my liquor. Just don't step on my new blue suede shoes. The shoes stand for a young man's pride and style. The opening ("one for the money...") is a traditional children's countdown before a race, and "cat" is slang for a cool guy.
nl: Carl Perkins (Carl. Perkins.), 1932 to 1998, grew up on a farm in Tennessee, loved the blues, and after hearing Elvis on the radio he modeled his style on Presley's and was signed by Sun in 1955.
Unlike Elvis, he wrote songs and played lead guitar.
His own song, Blue Suede Shoes, from 1956, was number two on both the pop and rhythm and blues charts and number one country.
In the listening guide, it's a twelve bar blues based song at about 168 beats per minute, with some choruses stretched to sixteen bars.
Most choruses begin with stop time, and the band is hollow body electric guitar, acoustic rhythm guitar, slapped stand up bass, and drums played on the rim.
The singer values his blue suede shoes, and dancing in them, above everything else in his life.
On the way to receive a gold record for the song, Perkins was badly injured in a car accident that killed his brother and his manager, and by the time he recovered, rockabilly was fading.
Blue Suede Shoes, by Carl Perkins (Carl. Perkins.). Rockabilly, 1956.

n: The Beatles covered several of his songs, Paul McCartney featured him on an album, and the eighties rockabilly revival band the Stray Cats took much of their style from him.
Here are the Stray Cats.
Rock This Town, by Stray Cats. Rockabilly revival, 1981.
Jerry Lee Lewis (Jerry. Lee. Lewis.), 1935 to 2022, was a pianist and singer whose rock career was short but influential.
He grew up in Louisiana listening to country and blues, and, as a cousin of the preacher Jimmy Swaggart, gospel.
After hearing Elvis's Sun records, he signed with Sun, and like Haley and Elvis he covered blues songs by African American musicians: Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On was first recorded by Big Maybelle.
Unlike them, he didn't clean up the sexual lyrics, and even added to them.

He played honky-tonk piano with tremendous energy, his right hand sweeping across the keys in glissandos while his left hand pounded a pumping bass line, and on stage he kicked away the bench and jumped on top of the piano, earning the nickname The Killer.
His career was ruined when the public learned he had married his thirteen year old third cousin without divorcing his second wife.
Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On, by Jerry Lee Lewis (Jerry. Lee. Lewis.). Rockabilly, 1957.
Summertime Blues, by Eddie Cochran, 1958.
Rockabilly.
Cochran was a young rockabilly star who played and sang every part on this record himself, through overdubbing.
Listen for the instrumental breaks between his lines, and the deep voice he uses to play the boss, his parents, and a congressman.
