items.lyr: A teenager complains about his summer: he has to work, and when he asks his boss for time off, the boss says no. His parents won't let him use the car because he didn't work late. He even writes to his congressman, who says he's too young to vote. "Raise a fuss, raise a holler" means complain loudly, and "there ain't no cure for the summertime blues" means nobody will help him.
nl: Rockabilly spread quickly to other artists.
Eddie Cochran (Eddie. Cochran.), 1938 to 1960, had a short career but a lasting influence, and he adopted the tough guy image of James Dean and Marlon Brando.
His hits came from experiments with overdubbing, where he played and sang all the parts himself, a technique invented by Les Paul in the early fifties.
Cochran's biggest hit was Summertime Blues, number eight on the pop charts in 1958.
In the listening guide, at about 152 beats per minute, it alternates A and B sections, and Cochran overdubbed the lead vocals, acoustic rhythm guitar, string bass, hand claps, and drums.
The repeating rockabilly rhythm has four even beats with a double accent on both halves of the second beat, and instrumental breaks draw attention to parts of the vocal line.
The singer is in agony because, when he should be having fun, everyone is making him work.
Summertime Blues, by Eddie Cochran (Eddie. Cochran.). Rockabilly, 1958.

n: Cochran saw rockabilly dying with the rise of teen idols, and his last hit, Three Steps to Heaven, wasn't rockabilly at all, but had a lightly strummed guitar, a doo-wop style vocal group, and very little backbeat.
He was killed in a car accident in England in 1960.
Three Steps to Heaven, by Eddie Cochran (Eddie. Cochran.). Pop, 1960.
Overdubbing, the technique behind Cochran's hits, was invented by the guitarist Les Paul, recording with his wife Mary Ford.
How High the Moon, by Les Paul & Mary Ford. Pop, 1951.
Gene Vincent (Gene. Vincent.), 1935 to 1971, was with Cochran in that accident and survived.

He grew up in Virginia singing white gospel, then formed a rockabilly group called the Blue Caps, and Capitol Records signed them as competition for Elvis, using an echo effect to imitate the Sun sound.
His image was rougher than Elvis's, and because a navy leg injury kept him from Elvis's hip movements, he conveyed sexual desperation through breathy vocals instead.
Be-Bop-A-Lula, from 1956, was his biggest hit.
Be-Bop-A-Lula, by Gene Vincent & His Blue Caps (Gene. Vincent. &. His. Blue. Caps.). Rockabilly, 1956.
Buddy Holly (Buddy. Holly.), 1936 to 1959, from Lubbock, Texas, turned to rock after seeing Elvis perform in 1955.
He and his drummer, Jerry Allison, formed the Crickets and recorded their first hit, That'll Be the Day, in 1957.
Holly was no Elvis imitator: he wrote much of his own music, his witty, personal style appealed to men as well as women, and his light voice had a trademark hiccup.
Instead of leather jackets, he wore suits, ties, and horn rimmed glasses.
That'll Be the Day, by Buddy Holly & The Crickets (Buddy. Holly. &. The. Crickets.). Rock and roll, 1957.
Peggy Sue, by Buddy Holly, 1957.
Rock and roll.
Holly was a singer, guitarist, and songwriter from Lubbock, Texas, and one of the first rock guitarists to play a solid body electric guitar.
Listen for the nonstop tom tom drumming, the hiccups in his voice, and the guitar solo suddenly bursting out louder.
items.lyr: A simple love song: if you knew Peggy Sue, you'd understand why he loves her so much. He repeats her name and says she's pretty, and that he longs for her. The word play and repetition matter more than any story.
nl: The Crickets had the same lineup as many later groups, including the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, both of which covered Holly's songs, and Holly was one of the first rock guitarists to play a solid body electric guitar.
The listening guide is Peggy Sue, from 1957, number three pop and number two rhythm and blues, which combines blues and country characteristics.
It's a twelve bar blues at about 148 beats per minute, with drums playing an energetic pattern on the tom toms with little or no backbeat.
Holly strums quietly during the verses, then plays a louder strummed solo influenced by Chuck Berry, and his vocal hiccup is clearest in the later choruses.
He may have overdubbed the rhythm guitar himself.
The song is about his unrequited love for a girl named Peggy Sue.
Peggy Sue, by Buddy Holly (Buddy. Holly.). Rock and roll, 1957.

n: Late in 1958, Holly moved to New York and began changing his style toward the new pop trend, and his last hit, It Doesn't Matter Anymore, was written by Paul Anka and recorded with strings.
He went on one more tour, with the Big Bopper, Ritchie Valens, and Dion, and with Waylon Jennings in his band.
The Big Bopper, Valens, and Holly all died in a plane crash on February third, 1959, a date rock fans have never forgotten.
Here's the Big Bopper.
Chantilly Lace, by The Big Bopper. Rock and roll, 1958.
The Everly Brothers (Everly. Brothers.), Don and Phil, were one of the few country influenced rock groups to stay popular from the late fifties into the early sixties.

Their closely harmonized tenor voices were accompanied by their own rhythm guitars, and their sound was smoother and fuller than Sun rockabilly, with voices sliding up to high notes, almost on the verge of tears.
Their hits included Bye Bye Love, All I Have to Do Is Dream, and Cathy's Clown, and their vocal style influenced many singers.
Bye Bye Love, by The Everly Brothers (Everly. Brothers.). Rock and roll, 1957.
The book ends the chapter with a box on early electric guitars.
Early jazz guitarists like Charlie Christian and T-Bone Walker played hollow body guitars with electric pickups attached.
Urban blues guitarists wanted more punch, so they chose thinner, semisolid guitars, like B.B. King's Gibson, which he named Lucille.

Les Paul and others then made the whole body solid, and Leo Fender's Telecaster, Gibson's Les Paul, and Fender's Stratocaster, which Buddy Holly played, became the standard guitars of sixties rock, played by Eric Clapton and Jimi Hendrix.
Here's B.B. King on Lucille.
The Thrill Is Gone, by B.B. King. Blues, 1969.
To recap chapter four.
Rock clearly began in blues and rhythm and blues, and the name rock and roll was first used for rhythm and blues.

By the fifties, new styles had emerged that were something more: blues and gospel based music by African American artists such as Fats Domino, Chuck Berry, and Little Richard, who added country and other influences, and blues songs covered by country musicians such as Bill Haley, Elvis Presley, and Buddy Holly.
However we label it, this fifties rock is the music on which the rest of rock history is built.
End of chapter four.
Before chapter five, the book introduces the decade of the sixties.

The decade began with optimism under the young president John F. Kennedy, who set the goal of putting a man on the moon, reached in 1969, but his fight against communism brought the Bay of Pigs invasion and the Cuban missile crisis, and he was assassinated in 1963.
The civil rights movement grew: in 1960, four African American students sat down at a whites only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and peaceful sit-ins spread across the country.
Riots followed in many cities, and both Malcolm X and Doctor Martin Luther King were assassinated, in 1965 and 1968.

There were also legal victories: the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act after King's march from Selma to Montgomery, Thurgood Marshall becoming the first African American Supreme Court justice, and the 1968 Housing Act.
The Vietnam War was the most controversial issue of all, and by 1966 rising casualties turned many Americans against it, with protests on college campuses.
Other movements began too: environmentalism, with Rachel Carson's Silent Spring, women's liberation, with Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique, and the hippie movement.
Much of the hippie optimism ended with the drug related deaths of Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, and Jim Morrison, and with a killing at the Rolling Stones' Altamont festival in 1969.
Chapter five: Teen-Styled Rock Music.

The point of this chapter is how, between 1957 and the mid sixties, rock was tamed into clean, wholesome pop for young teens, through teen idols, professional songwriters, and big studio productions, while the West Coast surf bands kept playing their own instruments.
By 1960, most of the strongest performers of mid fifties rock had stopped performing.

Carl Perkins stayed out of music after his car accident, Little Richard entered the ministry, Jerry Lee Lewis's records were banned, Elvis Presley was in the army, and Chuck Berry was on trial and later went to prison.
Buddy Holly, the Big Bopper, and Ritchie Valens died in the 1959 plane crash, and Eddie Cochran was killed in 1960.

Some had already sensed that pop was the future: Holly's and Cochran's last records were pop songs, while rockabilly artists who refused to change, like Gene Vincent and Ronnie Hawkins, left for England and Canada.
Payola means paying for airplay, and by the late fifties it meant paying radio and television programmers to play particular songs, so that money, rather than quality, decided what got played.
It wasn't illegal until after the scandal, but small independent labels depended on it.
The scandal was set off by songwriters' organizations.
The older organization, ASCAP, generally excluded blues, rhythm and blues, country, and rock writers, who joined its rival, BMI, formed in 1940.
As rock cut into its profits, ASCAP asked a congressional committee in 1958 to investigate bribes paid to disc jockeys, and many small labels that depended on payola went out of business.

Disc jockey Alan Freed had fought racism by giving African American artists as much airplay as he could, but he had also accepted a lot of payola, including a co-writing credit on Chuck Berry's Maybellene, and he lost his career.
Dick Clark, host of the teen dance show American Bandstand, was also investigated but escaped ruin, because his show was seen as a positive influence on teens.

American Bandstand brought Philadelphia pop music and dances to teenagers all over the country, mostly through clean cut, white teen idols, while the leather jackets and rebellious messages of rockabilly had no place there.
Tutti Frutti, by Little Richard, 1955. The original, to compare with the cover that follows.
It reached number seventeen on the pop charts and number two on the rhythm and blues charts.
Listen for his growling, no holds barred vocal with octave leap oohs, the jazz style walking bass, and the drummer's strongly accented backbeat.
items.lyr: Twelve bar blues form, with stop time breaks where the voice is alone. He sings about rocking with Sue (rocking was slang for sex) and hints that Daisy knows how to love him too, so he may not be true to Sue.
nl: Most teen idols, especially the men, sang in the style of the crooners of the twenties through the forties, such as Perry Como and Bing Crosby.
Pat Boone (Pat. Boone.), born in 1934, became popular singing pop ballads as well as covers of blues and rhythm and blues songs, changed to fit his clean cut, boy next door image.
While Carl Perkins and Elvis dared anyone to step on their blue suede shoes, Boone's trademark was clean white buck shoes.

The book compares the original Tutti Frutti, by Little Richard (Little. Richard.), which reached number seventeen pop and number two rhythm and blues, with Boone's cover, which reached number twelve pop.
Little Richard's version, from 1955, is a twelve bar blues at about 172 beats per minute.

It opens with a two bar introduction of nonsense syllables that shows off his no holds barred vocal style, punctuated by leaping oohs, and the last four bars of some choruses are sung over stop time breaks.
The piano plays even subdivisions against the uneven beat, with a jazz style walking bass, saxophone punctuations, and a strong backbeat on the drums.
In the lyrics, rocking with Sue was slang for sex, and Daisy knows how to love him too, hinting that he isn't faithful to Sue.
First, Little Richard's original.
Tutti Frutti, by Little Richard (Little. Richard.). Rock and roll, 1955.

n: Tutti Frutti, by Pat Boone, 1956.
Teen idol pop, a cover of Little Richard.
Boone was a clean cut, boy next door crooner, famous for his white buck shoes, and his version reached number twelve on the pop charts, higher than the original.
Listen for how he imitates Little Richard's rhythmic phrasing without his growl, the smoother and more polite voice, and the weaker backbeat.
items.lyr: Same twelve bar blues form and almost the same tempo. Boone removed the sexual references: no rocking, and instead of having two girlfriends he admits Daisy tempts him but stays true to Sue. He said he changed words that seemed too raw for him.
nl: Pat Boone's version, from 1956, is slightly faster, at about 176 beats per minute.
He imitates Little Richard's rhythmic singing and inflections, but without his growl, and his voice sounds smoother, more controlled, and polite.
A backup group sings ahs, the backbeat is less obvious, and the only jazz touch left is the tenor saxophone solo.
Boone removed the sexual references: there's no rocking with Sue, and instead of having two girlfriends, he admits Daisy tempts him but stays true to Sue.
Boone said he changed some words because they seemed too raw for him, and Little Richard joked that white kids put Pat Boone's record on the bed and hid his in the drawer.
The book argues Boone's Tutti Frutti counts as rock only because of its historical context: it represents the pop direction rock followed into the sixties.
Tutti Frutti, by Pat Boone (Pat. Boone.). Cover version, 1956.

n: Venus, by Frankie Avalon, 1959.
Teen idol pop.
Avalon was one of the Philadelphia teen idols introduced on American Bandstand, and Venus was number one for five weeks.
Listen for the very full production with orchestra, chorus, and drums, and the gentle, sincere mood of his crooning.
items.lyr: He is so desperate for romance that he prays to Venus, the Roman goddess of love, for a girlfriend, but he is also choosy and lists exactly what she should be like. A typical teen idol theme: puppy love and dreaming of the perfect mate.
nl: Movies and television supported the clean teen idol image.

American Bandstand introduced the Philadelphia teen idols Frankie Avalon, Fabian, and Bobby Rydell, who then starred in movies such as Beach Blanket Bingo, with Annette Funicello, and other idols included Ricky Nelson, Connie Francis, and Brenda Lee.
Most teen idols succeeded more through their looks and how much teenagers identified with them than through musical talent.
They usually lip synced to their records on TV and even in live shows, rarely played instruments, and generally didn't write songs.
Teen idol songs were as wholesome as the singers' images, mostly about puppy love and dreams of the perfect mate.
The listening guide is Venus, by Frankie Avalon (Frankie. Avalon.), from 1959, number one on the pop charts for five weeks.
It's at about 114 beats per minute, in A A B A form with an eight bar introduction of oohs from a chorus, and a full production with orchestra, chorus, and drums.
The mood is gentle and the singer very sincere.
In the lyrics, he's so desperate for romance that he prays to Venus, the Roman goddess of love, for a girlfriend, though he's also quite picky and lists exactly what he wants.
Venus, by Frankie Avalon (Frankie. Avalon.). Teen idol pop, 1959.

n: Paul Anka, born in 1941, was the exception among teen idols: he wrote many of his own hits, as well as songs for others, including Buddy Holly's It Doesn't Matter Anymore and Frank Sinatra's My Way.
Here's his own puppy love song.
Puppy Love, by Paul Anka. Teen idol pop, 1960.
Connie Francis was one of the most successful female singers of the teen idol era.
Where the Boys Are, by Connie Francis. Teen idol pop, 1961.
Because it featured teenage dancers, American Bandstand started or spread many dance crazes.
In the fifties, teens danced the bop, and its variations took animal names, like the Pony, the Chicken, and the Monkey.
Here's Danny and the Juniors' At the Hop.
At the Hop, by Danny & The Juniors. Rock and roll, 1957.
In 1960, a young Philadelphia performer named Ernest Evans covered a song called The Twist, by the blues singer Hank Ballard.
For his stage name, he chose Chubby Checker (Chubby. Checker.), a not so subtle variation on Fats Domino's name.
His version started a dance craze that lasted several years, with more Twist songs by Checker and others, including the Isley Brothers and Sam Cooke.
The Twist, by Chubby Checker (Chubby. Checker.). Dance pop, 1960.
Latin rhythms influenced jazz much more than rock, but one Latin rock hit was by the teen idol Ritchie Valens, 1941 to 1959: La Bamba, based on a traditional Mexican dance song.
La Bamba, by Ritchie Valens. Latin rock, 1959.

items.s: Breaking Up Is Hard to Do
n: Since pop singers rarely wrote songs, the pop boom created a need for professional songwriters.
Many pop hits between 1959 and 1963 were written and published in the Brill Building, at 1619 Broadway in New York, combining influences from gospel, doo-wop, and teen idol music.

Most of the writers worked in teams, the most famous being Howard Greenfield and Neil Sedaka, Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman, Gerry Goffin and Carole King, Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller, and Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich.
Sedaka, Mann, and King also sang some of their own hits.
Here's Neil Sedaka.
Breaking Up Is Hard to Do, by Neil Sedaka. Brill Building pop, 1962.
The producer George Shadow Morton worked with Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich on short storyline songs, unusual for pop, such as the Shangri-Las' Leader of the Pack, from 1964.
Leader of the Pack, by The Shangri-Las. Girl group, 1964.
Will You Love Me Tomorrow, by the Shirelles, 1960.
Brill Building pop, by a girl group.
It was written by Gerry Goffin and Carole King, and the Shirelles, unusual for the time, also wrote some of their own songs and had twelve top ten hits in four years.
Listen for Shirley Alston's lead backed doo wop style by the other Shirelles, and the orchestral strings playing the fills and the instrumental section.
items.lyr: AABA song form. The singer plans to sleep with her date and is unsure the relationship will last beyond that night. Carole King said it spoke for young women facing the double standard of the time: will you respect me in the morning?
nl: In early sixties pop, women were still mostly singers rather than instrumentalists, and trios and quartets of female singers, known as girl groups, became popular with teens.
The Shirelles (Shirelles.) placed twelve top ten hits on the pop charts between 1960 and 1963, and, unusually for pop singers of the time, did some of their own songwriting.
The listening guide is their first number one hit, Will You Love Me Tomorrow, from 1960, written by Carole King and her then husband, Gerry Goffin, a good example of the Brill Building pop sound.
It was number one pop for two weeks and number two rhythm and blues.
At about 138 beats per minute, in A A B A form with even subdivisions, Shirley Alston's lead is backed by the other Shirelles in doo-wop style.
The drums stress the backbeat with two quick notes on beat two and a single accent on beat four, and orchestral strings play fills at phrase endings and the lead in the instrumental section.
The singer plans to sleep with her date and isn't sure the relationship will last beyond that night.
Carole King said the song spoke for young women wondering whether he'd still respect them in the morning, cutting to the heart of the sexual double standard of the time.
Will You Love Me Tomorrow, by The Shirelles (Shirelles.). Girl group, 1960.

n: Phil Spector (Phil. Spector.), 1940 to 2021, was a Brill Building writer and producer whose productions were so distinctive that his style became known as the wall of sound.
He used so many instruments, overdubbed and mixed so thoroughly, that they formed a massive wall of instrumental color behind the vocals, and he disliked stereo, because it separated the instruments.
He loved the composer Richard Wagner, and added chimes, castanets, triangles, timpani, and gongs to an already full sound, calling his records symphonies for teens.
He owned his groups' names as well as the singers' contracts, so he could use any combination of singers and call them, for example, the Crystals.
When he did let a single instrument stand out, the effect was colorful, as in the flamenco style guitar on the Crystals' Uptown.
Uptown, by The Crystals. Girl group, 1962.
Be My Baby, by the Ronettes, 1963.
Girl group, produced by Phil Spector.
Spector's wall of sound overdubbed so many instruments, mixed together in mono, that they blend into one massive background, and he called his records symphonies for teens.
Listen for Ronnie singing the verses alone, the other two answering be my baby in the refrains, and the strings, guitars, keyboards, brass, saxophones, and percussion piled up behind them.
items.lyr: She promises her lover undying love and affection for all eternity, and asks him to be her baby. Spector later married Ronnie, the lead singer.
nl: The one group Spector kept as a regular trio was The Ronettes (Ronettes.), and he married their lead singer, Ronnie Bennett, in 1967.
The listening guide is Be My Baby, from 1963, number two pop and number four rhythm and blues.
At about 132 beats per minute, its wall of sound comes from overdubbed strings, guitars, several keyboards, brass, saxophones, and many percussion instruments.
The three Ronettes don't harmonize: Ronnie sings the verses alone, and the other two answer with be my baby in the refrains.
Low strings play the melody in an instrumental section, and a short break punctuated by percussion separates the third and fourth refrains.
In the lyrics, she promises her love and affection forever.
Be My Baby, by The Ronettes (Ronettes.). Girl group, 1963.

n: Spector was later asked to produce the Beatles' album Let It Be, and George Harrison's and John Lennon's solo albums, and in 1980 the Ramones.
In 2009, he was sentenced to prison for the shooting death of the actress Lana Clarkson.
Let It Be, by The Beatles. Rock, 1970.
While East Coast pop was about puppy love and teen dances, West Coast musicians developed their own danceable style, surf rock.

Surf vocals weren't based on the crooner tradition, and surf bands played their own instruments instead of using studio orchestras, in some ways a return to older rock played on guitars, bass, and drums.
Instrumental hits were more common in surf rock than in any earlier style, mostly with electric guitar in the lead, built on three sources: Duane Eddy, the Ventures, and Dick Dale.
Duane Eddy (Duane. Eddy.), born in 1938, created a style called twangy guitar by plucking the strings very close to the bridge, where they are tightest, for a strong, nasal attack.
He played repeated lead lines on the guitar's bass strings, with vibrato and echo, giving a wavering sound that may have reminded surf groups of moving water.
His first hit, Rebel-'Rouser, has the energy of gospel music and an instrumental call and response, in which a saxophone answers his guitar.
Rebel-'Rouser, by Duane Eddy (Duane. Eddy.). Instrumental rock, 1958.
The Ventures (Ventures.), from Tacoma, Washington, two guitarists, a bassist, and a drummer, were one of the most important early instrumental groups, with a sound clearly influenced by Eddy's twang.
They were one of the few surf groups to keep their following through the sixties and beyond, recording a version of the theme for the TV show Hawaii Five-O in 1969.
Hawaii Five-O, by The Ventures (Ventures.). Instrumental rock, 1969.
Misirlou, by Dick Dale and the Del Tones, 1961.
Instrumental surf rock.
Dale, the King of Surf Guitar, turned a Greek melody into a showpiece using the tremolo technique of Middle Eastern plucked instruments, which his Lebanese uncle taught him.
Listen for the very fast up and down picking that sustains each note while his other hand slides along the neck, and the amplifier reverb that gives the guitar a wet, surf sound.
items.lyr: No lyrics, only some wordless background vocals. The melody is broken up and varied to show off the guitar. Near the end the rock backbeat drops out for a Middle Eastern rhythm. A slower version was used in the film Pulp Fiction in 1994.
nl: Dick Dale (Dick. Dale.), born Richard Anthony Monsour, 1937 to 2019, was called the King of Surf Guitar, because he created a style copied by many surf groups.
In his version of the Greek melody Misirlou, from 1961, Dale developed a technique based on the tremolo of Middle Eastern plucked string instruments, meaning very fast repetitions of a note.
As his Lebanese uncle had taught him, he picked a string up and down very fast while sliding his other hand along the fingerboard, creating an impressive effect of speed, and added Eddy's twang.
In the listening guide, at about 192 beats per minute, the form is through composed, meaning the melody is broken up and varied rather than repeated in sections.
It opens with an unmeasured guitar introduction of fast tremolo picking and rapid descending scales, and amplifier reverb gives the guitar a wet sound, like being in the surf.
Once the drums enter they keep a fast beat with a backbeat, breaking five times for guitar solos, and near the end the backbeat drops out for a Middle Eastern rhythm.
Misirlou was used in the soundtrack of Pulp Fiction in 1994.
Misirlou, by Dick Dale & His Del-Tones (Dick. Dale. &. His. Del-Tones.). Surf rock, 1961.

n: Other surf instrumental groups, like the Marketts, the Chantays, and the Surfaris, took titles from surfing, and their very active drum solos with crashing cymbals imitated waves crashing on the beach.
Here's the Surfaris. Listen for the drum solo.
Wipe Out, by The Surfaris. Surf rock, 1963.
Sweet Little Sixteen, by Chuck Berry, 1958.
Rock and roll.
It reached number two on the pop charts and number one on the rhythm and blues charts, and the Beach Boys later reused its music for the next song.
Listen for Berry's guitar riff running through the song, the boogie woogie piano with long glissandos in the instrumental section, and the breaks where his voice is alone.
items.lyr: A sixteen year old girl tries to talk her parents into letting her go out to rock and roll. The verses name cities across the country where the good rock shows are.
nl: The Beach Boys (Beach. Boys.) were formed in Hawthorne, California, by three brothers, Brian, Carl, and Dennis Wilson, their cousin Mike Love, and a neighbor, Alan Jardine.

They were more than a surf group from the start: guitarist Carl Wilson used Eddy's twang and Dale's tremolo, but also imitated Chuck Berry's riffs, and Brian Wilson (Brian. Wilson.), the main writer and producer, based the group's harmonies on the jazz vocal group the Four Freshmen.

Their 1963 hit Surfin' U.S.A. had the same melody, chords, and form as Sweet Little Sixteen, a 1958 hit by Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.), and although Wilson first claimed the writing credit, the credit and royalties eventually went to Berry.
The listening guide compares the two.
Berry's version is at about 176 beats per minute, with uneven subdivisions, a strong backbeat, a guitar riff running through most of the song, and a boogie woogie piano solo with long glissandos.
Its sixteen bar verses are built from an antecedent phrase and a consequent phrase, two phrases on the same chords where the second sounds more final.
The lyrics are about a sixteen year old girl begging her parents to let her go out to rock and roll, naming cities with good rock music.
First, Chuck Berry's original.
Sweet Little Sixteen, by Chuck Berry (Chuck. Berry.). Rock and roll, 1958.

n: Surfin U S A, by the Beach Boys, 1963.
Surf rock, with vocals.
It has the same melody, chords, and form as Sweet Little Sixteen. Brian Wilson first claimed the writing credit, but it was eventually given to Chuck Berry.
Listen for the Four Freshmen style vocal harmonies, the imitation of Berry's guitar riff, and the organ and then guitar in the instrumental section.
items.lyr: A song about surfing and surfers. The singer wishes everyone in the country had an ocean and could have fun like the surfers in California, Australia, and Hawaii. Beach names take the place of the cities in Berry's song.
nl: The Beach Boys' version is a little slower, at about 164, with mostly even subdivisions, a strong backbeat, an imitation of Berry's guitar riff rhythm, and an organ and guitar solo.
Its antecedent and consequent phrases match Berry's closely, and the book suggests singing one of Berry's phrases followed by one of theirs to hear that Berry deserved the credit.
The lyrics wish that everyone in the country had an ocean, so they could surf like the surfers in California, Australia, and Hawaii, with surf spots replacing the cities in Berry's song.
Surfin' U.S.A., by The Beach Boys (Beach. Boys.). Surf music, 1963.

n: As Brian Wilson learned more about studio production, his records came close to the fullness of Spector's wall of sound, and he expanded the group beyond beach songs to school spirit and fast cars.
In 1966 he had a nervous breakdown and stopped touring, but kept writing, producing, and recording, and that year he made the Beach Boys' most important album, Pet Sounds.

All its songs were connected by a theme, the hopes, dreams, and anxieties of a young person growing up, and it sent rock albums in a new direction, inspiring the Beatles' Sgt. Pepper and other concept albums.
Here's one of its songs.
God Only Knows, by The Beach Boys (Beach. Boys.). Pop rock, 1966.
To recap chapter five.
In the late fifties and early sixties, much of what was called rock and roll changed from the energetic blues and country based sound of the mid fifties to a gentler pop sound called teen idol pop.

This happened because established songwriters resented competition from rock musicians who wrote their own songs, because much rock was recorded on small labels hurt by the payola scandal, and because many parents objected to rock's rebellious, sexy lyrics and dances.
Teen pop was written for young teens, marketed through movies and radio, and often backed by orchestras instead of guitars, bass, and drums, with the backbeat largely gone.
By the early sixties, the West Coast surf style became popular: surf bands played their own instruments, but their songs were still lighthearted celebrations of youth.
The Beach Boys eventually left surf behind, creating complex studio productions like Spector's wall of sound.
End of chapter five.
